clinical_category: Oncology clinical trials - informed consent and randomization
blueprint_topic: Informed consent / client rights / research participation
stem: A client is reviewing the informed-consent form for a randomized phase 3 cancer treatment trial that compares an investigational treatment with the current standard treatment. Which client statement indicates correct understanding?

options.A: I may receive either the investigational treatment or the standard treatment because assignment is by chance, and I can still choose to leave the study later.
options.B: Because this is phase 3, I am guaranteed to receive the investigational treatment if I sign the consent form.
options.C: If I am assigned to the standard-treatment group, I will receive no active cancer treatment because the comparison group is always untreated.
options.D: Once I sign the consent form, I must remain in the trial until the study ends even if I later change my mind.

rationale: A is correct. NCI states that phase 3 treatment trials compare an investigational treatment with the current standard treatment. In randomized trials, assignment is by chance; neither the participant nor the doctor chooses the treatment group. NCI informed-consent guidance also states that research participation is voluntary and that a participant may leave the study after signing the consent form. B is incorrect because enrollment does not guarantee assignment to the investigational arm. C is incorrect because, in the basic cancer-treatment trial design described by NCI, the control group receives standard treatment rather than no treatment; NCI also notes that placebos are rarely used in cancer treatment trials and are not routinely substituted for effective standard therapy. D is incorrect because signing the consent form does not surrender the participant's right to withdraw.
educational_objective: Verify that a client considering a randomized phase 3 cancer treatment trial understands random assignment, the role of standard-treatment comparison, and the continuing voluntary right to withdraw after consent.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: How Do Clinical Trials Work?; Understanding Informed Consent Forms; NCI Dictionary of Cancer Terms — randomization and phase III clinical trial
source_version_date: Understanding Informed Consent Forms updated 2024-11-03; current NCI clinical-trial and Dictionary resources accessed 2026-08-18

source_claim_supported: Phase 3 cancer treatment trials compare investigational and standard treatment; randomization assigns participants by chance rather than participant/physician choice; cancer treatment trials generally preserve active standard treatment in the comparison structure; informed consent is voluntary and participants retain the right to withdraw.

correction_summary: Rebuilt the source's phase-definition recall item into an informed-consent comprehension scenario. The final item preserves the verified phase 3 comparison concept but requires the nurse to recognize correct understanding of randomization, standard-treatment assignment, and the client's continuing right to withdraw. The Management of Care mapping is now tied to exact 2026 NCSBN informed-consent and client-rights content.
audit_findings: Fresh NCI review directly supports phase 3 comparison with current standard therapy and random assignment by chance; neither participant nor physician chooses the group in a randomized trial.
Fresh NCI informed-consent guidance directly supports voluntary participation and the right to leave after signing; the client does not sign away research-participant rights.
The stem explicitly states that this phase 3 trial is randomized, avoiding an unsupported claim that every possible phase 3 design must use identical randomization procedures.

Distractors address common clinically meaningful misconceptions—guaranteed investigational access, no active treatment in the comparator arm, and irrevocable consent—rather than weak phase-label trivia.
Independent adversarial review found one uniquely correct statement with no second answer, cueing, placebo overgeneralization, phase misclassification, source-locator defect, or unresolved conflict.
